about_text.value: Yusuf Lin, a recent convert from Chang'an, sits for the grueling Kalam examination to become a qadi in Bukhara. Eight lanterns illuminate eight trials testing legal reasoning, divine justice, free will, created speech, and the hidden relation between judge and witness. But Yusuf discovers that the ninth lantern remains unlit—reserved for those who realize the court itself must become evidence.

Yusuf can try to solve it and fail gloriously, or admit its impossibility. Yusuf becomes a model qadi—orderly, predictable, just within bounds. His judgments are never overturned but rarely remembered. He administers justice like water: necessary, invisible, taken for granted until it fails. The ninth lantern remains unlit.

Yusuf's name becomes legend—a qadi who judged by spirit over letter, whose decisions became poetry. Scholars argue whether he was wise or reckless. In taverns and caravanserais, his verdicts are recited with wine. The ninth lantern burns bright but flickers unpredictably.

Yusuf creates a new school of thought—the Bukhara Method—where precedents are living things that breathe and change. Future judges cite him, then contradict him, then cite his contradictions. He becomes the tradition he sought to transcend. The ninth lantern illuminates endless mirrors.

Yusuf discovers the Witness Without Name was himself all along—his Chinese self watching his Muslim self. His judgments become testimonies, each verdict an act of witness against his own biases. He never stops examining himself. The ninth lantern burns within.

Yusuf admits that every judgment distributes fault—the judge, the court, the law, even the victim. His famous decision: 'I cannot clear your name because guilt belongs to us all.' He resigns rather than continue distributing blame he refuses to bear alone.

Yusuf declares amnesty for all minor debts in his jurisdiction. The wealthy protest; the poor celebrate. When asked to justify, he says only: 'Sometimes silence is the fairest verdict.' He spends his days in a mosque garden, teaching nothing but listening.

Yusuf refuses all official positions. Instead, he becomes a wandering mediator—resolving disputes in market squares and caravan camps without formal authority. His judgments carry no legal weight but more binding force than any court decree. Justice beyond jurisdiction.

Yusuf recognizes that Shaykh Ibrahim is taking the same exam, testing whether he can pass a student who sees too much. Yusuf offers to switch places—to be examined as judge rather than candidate. The Shaykh smiles for the first time. Both pass. The ninth lantern illuminates two faces.
